explain.title: Mental multiplication: 43 times 6
paragraphs: Start with what working memory is supposed to be. Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed it because the older picture of short-term memory was too simple. In that older picture, short-term memory was mostly a waiting room where information sat until it was used or lost. Working memory is a limited-capacity system for the temporary storage and manipulation of information for complex tasks such as comprehension, learning and reasoning. Storage keeps something on hand briefly, and manipulation works on it. The hard part to grasp is that both have to happen at the same moment and draw on one shared, limited capacity.

Multiplying 43 times 6 in your head is a small, concrete case of exactly that. Walk through it slowly. First you picture the whole problem, 43 times 6, and keep it in mind so later steps can return to it. Then you multiply 3 by 6, which gives 18. Now comes the moment that matters: you hold the 8 in memory as the ones digit, and you carry the 1 over to the 4. Next you multiply 6 by 4 to get 24, and you add the carried 1 to get 25. Finally you combine that 25 with the 8 that has been held all along, and the answer is 258.

Look at what each piece of that work is doing. Keeping the 8 alive while everything else goes on is storage. Carrying, multiplying and adding are active processes, because each one changes the information. The trap is to think working memory only holds things, as if it were a shelf. But the 8 has to last through several steps while other operations run, so the answer depends on storage and processing working together, which is exactly the job of working memory.

That is why losing any stored piece breaks the answer. If the 8 slips away while you work on the tens, or if the carried 1 is never added, the result comes out wrong. So mental arithmetic is a direct test of working memory.

explain.title: Tower of Hanoi with subgoals
paragraphs: Newell and Simon (1956) looked at problem solving as a search that happens between the posing of the problem and its solution. Every problem has an initial state, intermediate states along the way, and a goal state, and operators are the rules that say which moves are allowed and take you from one state to another. In the Tower of Hanoi, the stack of three disks starts on the first peg and must end in the same order on the third. Disks move one at a time, only when nothing is on top, and never onto a smaller disk.

The goal is easy to picture, and that is what makes people go wrong. The stack cannot move all at once, so you cannot head straight for the goal. Smaller disks keep having to get out of the way, and the middle peg serves as a temporary parking spot. The moves explode as disks are added: with 64 disks it would take a trillion years, even at one correct move per second.

Means-end analysis is the strategy that tames this. It aims to reduce the differences between the initial state and the goal state, and it relies on subgoals, which are smaller goals that create intermediate states closer to the goal. Here the main difference is that the whole stack is on the wrong peg, and the largest disk cannot move until the disks above it are cleared. So the first subgoal is to free the large disk: the smallest disk goes from the first peg to the third, and the middle disk goes from the first peg to the middle peg. The second subgoal is to free the third peg: the smallest disk moves from the third peg onto the middle disk, so the two smaller disks sit legally together on the middle peg. The third subgoal is to move the large disk onto the third peg, where it is in its final place.

Notice that putting the smallest disk on the third peg and then taking it off looks wasteful. That detour is what frees the space the large disk needs, and means-end analysis accepts such detours when they remove an obstacle. Reaching the third subgoal is not finishing: the same strategy still has to move the two smaller disks onto the large one.

explain.title: Mutilated checkerboard
paragraphs: A checkerboard has 64 squares and can be completely covered by 32 dominoes, with each domino covering 2 neighboring squares. The mutilated checkerboard problem removes two opposite corners and asks whether the remaining 62 squares can be covered with 31 dominoes. This is hard because the numbers seem to fit: 31 dominoes at two squares each cover exactly 62 squares. The arithmetic alone suggests a covering exists, so people start laying dominoes down one at a time, and that could take a very long time and could never prove that a covering is impossible.

The answer is no, and the colors of the squares hold the key. Neighboring squares are always different colors, so every domino covers one dark square and one light square. Opposite corners share the same color, so removing them leaves 32 squares of one color and 30 of the other. Thirty-one dominoes would need 31 squares of each color, so a full covering is impossible. Once the board is represented by its colors, a single count settles the question before any domino is placed.

The key, then, is understanding two things: each domino covers two squares, and those squares must be of different colors. Conditions in the experiment differed in how much information was given about the squares. Condition 1 was a blank board, condition 2 a colored board, condition 3 wrote the words black and pink on the squares, and condition 4 wrote the words bread and butter. The bread and butter condition emphasized the difference between the squares, since bread and butter naturally come in pairs, one of each, and participants solved it twice as fast as the blank condition. The board and dominoes were identical throughout, so only the representation changed.

Think-aloud protocols show this happening. Participants get the problem after realizing that the words bread and butter are important; before that they talk about laying down dominoes, and afterward they talk about pairing the two kinds of squares. That is similar to the Gestalt idea of a representational shift. Equal area, 62 squares and 31 dominoes, is therefore never enough: the covering also needs equal numbers of the two colors.

explain.title: Chain problem
paragraphs: The chain problem was one of the insight problems used by Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987), who designed an experiment to distinguish insight from noninsight problems. The triangle problem and the chain problem were the insight problems, and algebra problems were the noninsight ones. Participants gave warmth judgments every 15 seconds, rating how close they felt to the answer. Metcalfe and Wiebe expected that in insight problems people would not be very good at predicting how near they were to a solution, because if insight comes suddenly the solver should feel far away right until the answer arrives.

Here is the problem. You have four short pieces of chain, each with three links, and you must join them into a single closed loop. Opening a link costs 2 cents, closing a link costs 3 cents, and you have only 15 cents to spend. The obvious plan is to open one link on each piece and use it to join the next piece. Work it out slowly: that is four links, each costing 2 to open and 3 to close, which is 20 cents, and that goes over budget. Opening and closing one link costs 5 cents, so 15 cents allows only three links, and the obvious plan needs four.

The answer comes from seeing the parts differently. Open all three links of one piece, and use those three open links to join the other three pieces into a loop, closing each once. That costs 3 times (2 plus 3), which is exactly 15 cents. The shift is treating one whole piece of chain as a set of connectors instead of as a piece to be joined.

Neither this answer nor the triangle answer comes from gradual improvement. Each requires leaving the obvious approach behind, and both problems look simple, which makes the obvious approach hard to give up. This is the kind of restructuring that Gestalt psychologists linked to insight. Steadily rising warmth would mean gradual progress, while low warmth followed by a sudden jump means insight, and that is the pattern these problems were chosen to produce.

explain.title: Triangle problem
paragraphs: The triangle problem is the second of the insight problems used by Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987). They compared insight problems, the triangle and chain problems, with noninsight algebra problems, and they asked participants for warmth judgments every 15 seconds, rating from cold to hot how close they felt to the answer. Their expectation was that with noninsight problems, which involve a more methodical process, people know how close they are because every finished step brings the answer visibly closer. With insight problems, people should not be very good at predicting how near they are, because the solution arrives suddenly.

The task is to move three of the blue dots to make the triangle point to the bottom of the page. The triangle has ten dots arranged in rows of one, two, three and four, with the point on top, and the rule is that seven of the dots stay where they are while only three move. This is hard because the problem looks simple, which makes the obvious approach hard to give up, and the obvious approach does not work.

Walk through the answer slowly. The top dot, the one at the point, goes below the middle of the bottom row. The two ends of the bottom row go up beside the row of two dots. Count what you have now. The row that held two dots now has four, and below it sit the rows of three, two and one. The rows run four, three, two and one, so the triangle points down, and only three dots moved.

Nothing about this comes from gradual improvement. You cannot get nearer by small adjustments; you have to give up the picture of an upward triangle and see the dots as parts that can be regrouped. That is the restructuring that Gestalt psychologists linked to insight, and it explains why warmth stays low and then jumps instead of rising steadily.

explain.title: Water-jug problems and mental set
paragraphs: A mental set is a preconceived notion about how to approach a problem, based on a person's past experiences with the problem or with similar problems. It is a broader form of fixation, and the idea is that a method that worked before gets used again, even when a better method is available. The water-jug problem reveals how a mental set works. The task is to figure out how to obtain a required volume of water, given three empty jars for measuring. Each problem gives the capacities of jugs A, B and C and a final desired quantity, in quarts, and only filling, pouring and emptying are allowed.

Take problem 1, where the jugs hold 21, 127 and 3 quarts and the target is 100. Fill jug B with 127 quarts and pour from B into A until A is full, which leaves 106 quarts in B. Then pour from B into C until C is full, empty C and fill it once more, which leaves exactly 100 quarts in B. So the formula is B minus A minus twice C, which is 127 minus 21 minus 2 times 3, or 100. The same formula solves each of the early problems.

The trouble is what that success does to you. Participants started applying the formula automatically, and that automatic habit is the mental set. It forms because the formula keeps working. Then the later problems test the habit. Problem 7 has jugs of 15, 39 and 3 quarts and a target of 18. The long formula still works, giving 39 minus 15 minus 6, but simply adding A and C, 15 plus 3, gives 18 directly. Problem 8 has jugs of 28, 59 and 3 and a target of 25, which A minus C solves directly, 28 minus 3, even though the familiar formula also works.

What the experiment shows is that the mental set inhibited participants from using the simpler solutions, and people who had not worked through the earlier problems found the short methods far more often. A set speeds up solving when problems are alike, but once the problems change, the same set hides the easier paths. Past success can therefore become an obstacle in its own right. The familiar method is not wrong in problems 7 and 8; it is just that it blocks the simpler one.
